questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

A) What does the metacharacter `?` mean in a regular expression?
questions.answer: Zero or one occurrence of the preceding atom (the preceding character, bracket expression or group is optional).
questions.grading: Must say zero-or-one AND that it applies to the preceding item. "Any single character" is the GLOB meaning of `?` (that is `.` in a regex) and is wrong.

rubric.item: Zero or one instance of the preceding atom

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

A) What does the metacharacter `+` mean in a regular expression?
questions.answer: One or more occurrences of the preceding atom.
questions.grading: Must be one-or-more of the preceding item. "Zero or more" is `*` (wrong).

rubric.item: One or more instances of the preceding atom

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

B) Provide a regular expression that matches all strings that start and end with a lowercase English letter.
questions.answer:
```
^[a-z](.*[a-z])?$
```

This matches a single lowercase letter (e.g. `a`) as well as longer strings such as `a1b`.
questions.grading: Exactly correct: `^[a-z](.*[a-z])?$` or `^[a-z]$|^[a-z].*[a-z]$`. The posted solution also lists `^[a-z]+$` and `^[a-z]*[a-z]$` as "correct" (those only match strings made entirely of lowercase letters, e.g. not `a1b`, so they read the question as "lowercase-letter strings"), and says `^[a-z].*[a-z]$` was "sufficient for the quiz" even though it misses one-letter strings. Give the mark for any of these, but mention the single-letter edge case if it is missed. Missing anchors (`[a-z].*[a-z]`) loses the mark, as does a glob such as `[a-z]*[a-z]`.

rubric.item: Anchored regex requiring a lowercase letter at both the start and the end

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

B) Provide a regular expression that matches all strings that start with a digit and end with an uppercase English letter.
questions.answer:
```
^[0-9].*[A-Z]$
```

(A single character cannot be both a digit and an uppercase letter, so every match has at least two characters and `.*` in the middle is exactly right.)
questions.grading: Needs both anchors, `[0-9]` at the start, `[A-Z]` at the end and `.*` between. `^[0-9]+[A-Z]+$` is too narrow (rejects `1xQ`). `[[:digit:]]`/`[[:upper:]]` are fine.

rubric.item: `^[0-9].*[A-Z]$` or equivalent

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

C) Show how to create a Bash array `arr` that contains the values 1, 2, and 3.
questions.grading: No spaces around `=`, no commas. `arr=(1, 2, 3)` or `arr=[1 2 3]` is wrong. `declare -a arr=(1 2 3)` and assigning each `arr[0]=1` etc. are fine.

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

C) Show how to create a Bash array `names` that contains the two values `Ann Lee` and `Bo Li` (each value contains a space).
questions.grading: Each element must be quoted, otherwise word splitting makes four elements. No commas, no spaces around `=`.

rubric.item: `names=("Ann Lee" "Bo Li")` with each element quoted

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

D) Given a Bash array `arr`, show how to get the number of elements in `arr`.
questions.grading: `${#arr[@]}` or `${#arr[*]}`. `${#arr}` is the length of element 0 (wrong); `$#` is the argument count (wrong).

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

D) Given a Bash array `arr`, show how to append the value `4` to the end of `arr`.
questions.grading: `arr+=(4)` (or `arr[${#arr[@]}]=4`, fine for a contiguous array). `arr+=4` is wrong: it appends the text 4 to element 0.

rubric.item: `arr+=(4)` with the parentheses

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

E) Suppose that you have a variable `f` that stores the name of a file. Write a Bash `if` statement that prints the message `not readable` to standard output if the file whose name is stored in `f` is not a readable file.
questions.grading: Needs `!` and `-r` inside `[[ ]]` (`[ ! -r "$f" ]` fine), plus `then` and `fi`. Inside `[[ ]]` quoting `$f` is optional. Missing `; then` (when on one line) or `fi` loses the mark. `-e`/`-f` test something else.

rubric.item: Complete `if [[ ! -r $f ]]; then echo "not readable"; fi`

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

E) Suppose that you have a variable `d` that stores a name. Write a Bash `if` statement that prints the message `no such directory` to standard output if `d` is not the name of an existing directory.
questions.answer:
```bash
if [[ ! -d $d ]]; then echo "no such directory"; fi
```
questions.grading: Needs `! -d`, `then`, `fi`. `-e` is not enough (a regular file exists but is not a directory).

rubric.item: Complete `if [[ ! -d $d ]]; then ...; fi`

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

F) Fill in the blank in the following Bash `for` loop so that the loop processes each command line argument given to a script:

```bash
for ____________________; do
    # loop body not shown
done
```
questions.answer:
```bash
for arg in "$@"; do
    echo "$arg"    # loop body
done
```

The blank is `arg in "$@"`.
questions.grading: `arg in "$@"` (any variable name). Quotes around `$@` are needed so arguments with spaces stay whole; unquoted `$@` or `$*` loses the mark under course conventions. `for arg; do` (no `in` list) is also correct. `for (( i = 1; i <= $#; i++ ))` gives indexes, not arguments, unless the body is shown to use them.

rubric.item: `arg in "$@"` with quotes

questions.prompt:
Question 1 (1 mark each). Your answer for each of the following parts should be very brief.

F) Fill in the blank in the following Bash `for` loop so that the loop processes each element of an array `arr` (elements may contain spaces):

```bash
for ____________________; do
    # loop body not shown
done
```
questions.answer:
```bash
for elem in "${arr[@]}"; do
    echo "$elem"    # loop body
done
```

The blank is `elem in "${arr[@]}"`.
questions.grading: Must be `"${arr[@]}"` quoted. `${arr[@]}` unquoted splits elements with spaces; `"${arr[*]}"` gives one single string; `$arr` gives only element 0.

rubric.item: `elem in "${arr[@]}"` quoted

questions.prompt:
Question 4 (10 marks).

The selection sort algorithm for sorting an array `arr` of `n` integers can be described as follows:

```
for j=0, 1, 2, ..., n-1
   idx = minidx(j)
   swap arr[j] and arr[idx]
```

The function call `minidx(j)` finds the index of the minimum element in `arr` starting at index `j`
and going to the end of `arr`. For example, if `arr` is the array

```
[0, 3, 1, 4, 2]
```

then

```
minidx(0) returns 0
minidx(1) returns 2
minidx(2) returns 2
minidx(3) returns 4
minidx(4) returns 4
```

Complete the following Bash script so that it implements the selection sort algorithm to sort the
command line arguments provided to the script. The functions `sort` and `minidx` are the
selection sort algorithm and minimum index algorithm described above.

```bash
#!/bin/bash

function sort {
}

function minidx {
}

# places the command line arguments into arr and calls sort
arr=("$@")
sort

# print the sorted elements of arr on a single line after this comment
```

You may answer this question by providing implementations of the `sort` and `minidx` functions
and by showing how to print the elements of the sorted array on a single line.

No error checking is required. You may assume that the command line arguments provided to the
script are always integers.

You may choose how to call `minidx` and how to return a value from `minidx`.
questions.grading: Any correct way to return the index is fine: a global variable (dynamic scoping, as above) or printing it and capturing with `idx=$(minidx "$j")`. `return idx` is NOT acceptable as a general solution (exit status is 0-255) - deduct 1 mark. Comparison must be numeric: `(( ... < ... ))` or `[[ $a -lt $b ]]`; `[[ $a < $b ]]` is a STRING comparison (wrong for e.g. 10 vs 9) - deduct. The swap needs a temporary variable. `n` must be known before `sort` runs: the posted solution sets `n=${#arr[@]}` but only after the call to `sort` in its layout, so compute `n` inside the functions or before `sort` is called. Keeping the printed `function sort {` style is fine. Watch for `minidx` clobbering the caller's loop variable when both use the same global name (e.g. both use `i` without `local`). Print with `echo "${arr[@]}"` (or `${arr[*]}`).

rubric.item: minidx loops i from start+1 to n-1 over arr
minidx uses a numeric comparison and tracks the index of the smallest value
minidx returns the index via a global variable or echo + command substitution (not `return`)
sort loops j from 0 to n-1 and calls minidx with j
sort swaps arr[j] and arr[idx] correctly using a temporary
Prints the sorted array on one line with `echo "${arr[@]}"`

questions.prompt:
Question 4 (10 marks).

The selection sort algorithm for sorting an array `arr` of `n` integers into DESCENDING order (largest first) can be described as follows:

```
for j=0, 1, 2, ..., n-1
   idx = maxidx(j)
   swap arr[j] and arr[idx]
```

The function call `maxidx(j)` finds the index of the maximum element in `arr` starting at index `j`
and going to the end of `arr`. For example, if `arr` is the array

```
[0, 3, 1, 4, 2]
```

then

```
maxidx(0) returns 3
maxidx(1) returns 3
maxidx(2) returns 3
maxidx(3) returns 3
maxidx(4) returns 4
```

Complete the following Bash script so that it implements the selection sort algorithm to sort the
command line arguments provided to the script into descending order. The functions `sort_desc` and `maxidx`
are the selection sort algorithm and maximum index algorithm described above.

```bash
#!/bin/bash

function sort_desc {
}

function maxidx {
}

# places the command line arguments into arr and calls sort_desc
arr=("$@")
sort_desc

# print the sorted elements of arr on a single line after this comment
```

You may answer this question by providing implementations of the `sort_desc` and `maxidx` functions
and by showing how to print the elements of the sorted array on a single line.

No error checking is required. You may assume that the command line arguments provided to the
script are always integers.

You may choose how to call `maxidx` and how to return a value from `maxidx`.
questions.answer:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

sort_desc() {
    local n=${#arr[@]}
    local j tmp idx
    for (( j = 0; j < n; j++ )); do
        idx=$(maxidx "$j")          # maxidx prints its result
        tmp=${arr[j]}
        arr[j]=${arr[idx]}
        arr[idx]=$tmp
    done
}

maxidx() {
    local start=$1
    local n=${#arr[@]}
    local i
    local hi=$start
    for (( i = start + 1; i < n; i++ )); do
        if (( arr[i] > arr[hi] )); then
            hi=$i
        fi
    done
    echo "$hi"
}

# places the command line arguments into arr and calls sort_desc
arr=("$@")
sort_desc

# print the sorted elements of arr on a single line after this comment
echo "${arr[@]}"
```

Tested: `./sort.sh 0 3 1 4 2` prints `4 3 2 1 0`; `./sort.sh 12 9 100 1` prints `100 12 9 1`.
questions.grading: Same marking as the original. The comparison must be `>` (numeric). Returning the index with echo + `$( )` works because the subshell can still read `arr`; a global variable is also fine. `return` for the index is not acceptable. Swap needs a temporary.

rubric.item: maxidx loops i from start+1 to n-1
maxidx uses a numeric `>` comparison and tracks the index of the largest value
maxidx returns the index via echo + command substitution or a global
sort_desc loops j from 0 to n-1 calling maxidx j
Correct swap of arr[j] and arr[idx] with a temporary
Prints `"${arr[@]}"` on one line
